A model of the worksheet diagram

Three positive charges in a negative background.

Find the locations where the total electric potential is zero. Take V(∞) = 0. The reference length is a, and q > 0.

To explore the worksheet, the lesson treats each sign as one charge of magnitude q and uses the symmetric model shown here. Positions are estimated from the photograph; the negative clusters are represented by combined point charges.

Exact equations, approximate geometry.
The potential formula is exact for these five point charges. The contour lines are numerical approximations to its level sets. They are 2D slices of a 3D electrostatic potential.
ChargePosition (x/a, y/a)
Top negative cluster −2q(0, 2)
Upper positive +q(0, 1)
Left positive +q(−1, 0)
Right positive +q(1, 0)
Bottom negative cluster −3q(0, −0.6)

Net charge: −2q. Removing any one +q leaves a group with net charge −3q.

Method 01 · Mathematics

Add the voltage at each point.

Potential is a scalar: each charge contributes its signed value. Let X=x/a, Y=y/a, and v=Va/(kq), where k=1/(4πε₀).

V(P) = k Σqᵢrᵢ,   rᵢ = √[(x−xᵢ)²+(y−yᵢ)²]
v(X,Y) = 1√[X²+(Y−1)²] + 1√[(X+1)²+Y²] + 1√[(X−1)²+Y²]
        − 2√[X²+(Y−2)²] − 3√[X²+(Y+0.6)²].

An equipotential curve is the set of points satisfying v(X,Y)=c. Choose c=0 for the zero-voltage boundary. Because all five terms contribute, these loops are generally not circles.

v = 0v > 0v < 0

Click or tap the plot to inspect a point. Axes show X and Y. Contour values are normalized potential, not volts.

Potential inspector

Contributionqᵢ/q ÷ (rᵢ/a)

At a teal boundary, positive and negative contributions cancel. The field usually remains nonzero.

Anchor points you can calculate

Along X=0, the upper loop is found by solving this one-variable equation away from the charges:

1/|Y−1| + 2/√(1+Y²) − 2/|Y−2| − 3/|Y+0.6| = 0.
Vertical-axis crossings

Y ≈ 0.552412 and 1.307929

From the positive charge at Y=1: 0.447588a downward and 0.307929a upward.

Horizontal-axis crossings

X ≈ ±0.653900 and ±1.623385

These anchor the side loops at Y=0. Left–right symmetry gives the negative-X points.

How the numerical calculation works

Evaluate the full potential on a grid, find cells where v−c changes sign, interpolate the crossings, and join short contour segments. Near a charge, exclude a small singular region. For the axis anchors, bracket a sign change and bisect until the root converges. A finer grid improves contour accuracy; the root values above come from a separate one-dimensional solver.

For example, v(0,1.30) ≈ +0.1167 and v(0,1.32) ≈ −0.1710. A zero lies between them. Repeated bisection gives Y≈1.307929.

Method 02 · Intuition

Start far away. Let the circle deform.

Separate one positive charge

The other charges total −3q. When that group is compact compared with its distance from the selected +q and the boundary, replace it approximately by one effective −3q charge.

Find the starting circle

kq/r₊ − 3kq/rrest = 0   ⇒   rrest = 3r₊

A constant distance ratio gives an Apollonius circle. It encloses the selected positive charge, which is displaced from the circle’s centre.

Approach and separate the contributions

As distances become comparable to the size of the group, use its actual charge locations. Nearby negative charges tend to compress the boundary; nearby positive charges can extend or join positive-potential regions.

Check the total at each trial point

Transport a boundary point with the moving +q so its distance from that charge stays fixed. Add the other charges’ changed contributions. If the trial voltage becomes negative, shift toward higher potential; if it becomes positive, shift toward lower potential.

Why the distant boundary is a circle

Put +q at u=0 and the effective −3q at vector D, with length D. Then:

|u−D| = 3|u|
|u|² + (D·u)/4 − D²/8 = 0
|u+D/8|² = (3D/8)²

The circle’s centre is −D/8 relative to +q; its radius is 3D/8. It extends D/4 toward the negative group and D/2 away from it.

A precise version of “push the boundary”

For a small change, at an old zero point P:

δs ≈ δV / |E|

Here δs is measured along the old field direction, toward lower potential. This follows from 0≈δV+∇V·δr and E=−∇V.

Use consistent physical units. The same relation holds for normalized v and −∇v. It fails near E=0, where topology can change and loops may join or split. “Inward” and “outward” are local guides when the selected +q dominates the radial variation.

Explore · Three separate thought experiments

Bring a charge in yourself.

Only the gold-ringed charge moves. The full potential sum is recalculated at every slider position. The final positions, and therefore the final curves, are identical for every approach path.

The view zooms automatically. Compare the axis values and boundary distances below when judging size. Colored dots mark the first zero crossing along four rays from the moving charge; they are not physical particles.

RayZero distance / a
The horizontal upper approach can temporarily join two positive regions. Try the upper charge, select the horizontal path, and move close to the final position. Near X≈1.3, Y=1, a single zero loop surrounds both the moving +q and the lower-right +q. At the final positions they separate again. A diagonal approach avoids this particular close pass; it is easier to read.

Predict the final distortion

Upper positive

The −2q above compresses the top. The two side positives partly oppose the negative background below. The final loop extends farther downward than upward.

Left positive

The bottom −3q compresses the lower-right side. The upper positive supports an extension toward the upper gap; the outer-left boundary has more room.

Right positive

This is the mirror image of the left loop: compressed toward the bottom negative charge, with more room outward and upward.

These statements describe the final model. During approach, different contributions compete, so a particular boundary distance need not change monotonically.

From calculation to a hand sketch

Use a few points, then connect smoothly.

  1. Mark the five charge locations and exploit left–right symmetry.
  2. Place the axis crossings listed above. These give six reliable anchors.
  3. Use the four-ray distances in the approach lab at “Final” to estimate each loop’s top, bottom and sides.
  4. Connect the anchors with smooth curves. Check a few trial points by summing qᵢ/rᵢ; refine the boundary toward v=0.
  5. Shade positive potential inside the three loops and negative potential outside. Do not force them into exact circles or make them merge.

Draw electric-field directions

E = −∇V

Draw arrows perpendicular to equipotentials, toward lower voltage. At each final zero loop, the field points from its positive interior toward the negative exterior. A zero potential does not imply a zero field.

If an electron or proton is released

F = qtestE

A proton initially accelerates along the field; an electron initially accelerates opposite to it. Choose an off-axis point for a generally curved trajectory. The initial direction is normal to the equipotential.

A free particle’s later trajectory generally does not follow a field line: its velocity retains inertia. Calculate the full trajectory with m d²r/dt²=qtestE(r), rather than treating field lines as tracks.

What superposition does—and does not—mean

Add the signed potential values at the same point. Individual zero contours cannot be added or simply overlaid to get the final zero contour. The three approach experiments are different temporary arrangements; each ends at the same full arrangement.

Why equal and opposite charges gave a straight line earlier

For +Q and −Q, V=0 requires r₊=r₋: the perpendicular bisector in a plane. For unequal opposite charges, a constant ratio r₊/r₋≠1 gives a circle in 2D, or a sphere in 3D. Adding more charge locations generally changes the zero set into a noncircular curve.
